claim: The pre-Bötzinger complex (preBötC) putatively drives inspiratory breathing rhythms.
source: The brainstem pre-Bötzinger complex (preBötC) putatively drives inspiratory breathing rhythms (Smith et al., 1991; Feldman et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Smith et al., 1991; Feldman et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2013).

claim: Respiratory rhythms persist in reduced slice preparations that retain the preBötC and can be monitored via respiratory hypoglossal (XII) nerve discharge.
source: These rhythms persist in reduced slice preparations that retain the preBötC and can be monitored via respiratory hypoglossal (XII) nerve discharge, providing a powerful in vitro model of breathing behavior (Lieske et al., 2000; Koizumi et al., 2008; Funk and Greer, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lieske et al., 2000; Koizumi et al., 2008; Funk and Greer, 2013).

claim: Glutamatergic, peptidergic, and peptide receptor-expressing preBötC interneurons develop from a common set of precursors that express the homeobox gene Dbx1 during embryonic development.
source: Glutamatergic, peptidergic, and peptide receptor-expressing preBötC interneurons develop from a common set of precursors that express the homeobox gene Dbx1 during embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about developmental biology of preBötC neurons.

claim: Dbx1-derived interneurons in perinatal mice are inspiratory modulated.
source: Dbx1-derived interneurons (hereafter Dbx1 neurons) in perinatal mice are inspiratory modulated, and Dbx1-null mice die at birth without ever breathing (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).

claim: Dbx1-null mice die at birth without ever breathing.
source: Dbx1-derived interneurons (hereafter Dbx1 neurons) in perinatal mice are inspiratory modulated, and Dbx1-null mice die at birth without ever breathing (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).

claim: The destruction of approximately 120 rhythmic neurons irreversibly stopped respiratory rhythmogenesis in a previous study.
source: Previously, we estimated the cellular mass critical for respiratory rhythm generation by laser-ablating preBötC inspiratory interneurons identified by Ca2+ imaging. The destruction of ∼120 rhythmic neurons irreversibly stopped respiratory rhythmogenesis (Hayes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Hayes et al., 2012).

claim: Inspiratory rhythms in vivo and in vitro do not require synaptic inhibition.
source: inspiratory rhythms in vivo and in vitro do not require synaptic inhibition (Feldman and Smith, 1989; Brockhaus and Ballanyi, 1998; Kuwana et al., 2003; Ren and Greer, 2006; Fujii et al., 2007; Janczewski et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Feldman and Smith, 1989; Brockhaus and Ballanyi, 1998; Kuwana et al., 2003; Ren and Greer, 2006; Fujii et al., 2007; Janczewski et al., 2013).

claim: Cumulative destruction of Dbx1 preBötC neurons progressively decreased respiratory frequency until rhythm ceased after ablation of approximately 85 neurons.
source: As predicted, cumulative destruction of Dbx1 preBötC neurons progressively decreased respiratory frequency until rhythm ceased after ablation of ∼85 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cumulative Dbx1 cellular ablations diminished the amplitude of respiratory XII nerve discharge.
source: Surprisingly, cumulative Dbx1 cellular ablations also diminished the amplitude of respiratory XII nerve discharge, suggesting that Dbx1 preBötC neurons also influence motor output.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dbx1 preBötC neurons influence motor output.
source: Surprisingly, cumulative Dbx1 cellular ablations also diminished the amplitude of respiratory XII nerve discharge, suggesting that Dbx1 preBötC neurons also influence motor output.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ablations diminished XII nerve discharge amplitude.

claim: In simulations that assign only rhythm-generating function to preBötC neurons, cumulative ablations decreased frequency and stopped rhythmogenesis but at much lower tallies and without perturbing the output amplitude.
source: In simulations that assign only rhythm-generating function to preBötC neurons, cumulative ablations decreased frequency and stopped rhythmogenesis but at much lower tallies and without perturbing the output amplitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dbx1 neurons were detected and mapped within the preBötC, and then laser ablated individually, in sequence, while monitoring respiratory network functionality via XII motor nerve output.
source: Dbx1 neurons were detected and mapped within the preBötC, and then laser ablated individually, in sequence, while monitoring respiratory network functionality via XII motor nerve output.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Dbx1 neurons form a bilaterally symmetrical V-shape starting dorsally at the border of the XII motor nuclei and continuing ventrolaterally to the preBötC.
source: Viewed in the transverse plane of slices that expose the preBötC at their surface (i.e., preBötC-surface slices), Dbx1 neurons form a bilaterally symmetrical V-shape starting dorsally at the border of the XII motor nuclei and continuing ventrolaterally to the preBötC (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The overwhelming majority of Dbx1 preBötC neurons are inspiratory.
source: At the cellular level, identifying putative rhythmogenic neurons on the basis of fluorescent protein expression alone is acceptable because the overwhelming majority of Dbx1 preBötC neurons are inspiratory (e.g., Figure 1B) (Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Picardo et al., 2013) and visual evidence in Figure 1B.

claim: An average of 705 targets were detected in the preBötC.
source: Typically, we detected 26–50 Dbx1 neurons per focal plane per side (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) for a total average number of 705 targets in the preBötC (SD 119, SEM 59, range: 548 to 802, n = 8 slices).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Generally more than 90% of lesion attempts are successful.
source: Generally >90% of lesion attempts are successful (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Hayes et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research (Hayes et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).

claim: XII amplitude decreased steeply with the tally of ablated cells, and then stabilized at 44% of its pre-lesion value.
source: XII amplitude decreased steeply with the tally of ablated cells, and then stabilized at 44% of its pre-lesion value (SD 4%, SEM 1%, suction electrode recordings are reported in normalized arbitrary units).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Respiratory frequency continued to decrease throughout the ablation phase.
source: Frequency, however, continued to decrease (i.e., cycle period increased) throughout the ablation phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within the first dozen ablations, the average decrease in respiratory frequency was nearly twofold.
source: Initially, within the first dozen ablations, the average decrease in respiratory frequency was nearly twofold, and it continued to fall steeply until rhythm cessation (range of frequencies: 0.22–0.007 Hz, Figure 3B [inset shows bi-exponential increase in cycle period], n = 5 slices).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 3B.

claim: The regularity score of preBötC-surface slices measured 1–9 during the ablation phase.
source: The RS of preBötC-surface slices measured 1–9 during the ablation phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 3C.

claim: Respiratory rhythm ceased altogether after an average of 85 confirmed Dbx1 neuron ablations in preBötC-surface slices.
source: Respiratory rhythm ceased altogether after an average of 85 confirmed Dbx1 neuron ablations in preBötC-surface slices (SD 44, SEM 20, range 42–137, n = 5 slices), well before exhausting the average list of 705 targets per slice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ablations were bilateral and the tally reflects the sum of both sides.
source: These ablations were bilateral and the tally reflects the sum of both sides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: An average of 906 targets per slice were acquired in control slices.
source: We acquired 38–60 Dbx1 neuron targets per focal plane per side (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) for a total average of 906 targets per slice (SD 97, SEM 34, range: 722–1004, n = 8 slices).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amplitude of XII motor output decreased to 77% of control over the course of the ablation phase in control slices.
source: The amplitude of XII motor output decreased to 77% of control (SD 2%, SEM 1%, normalized arbitrary units) over the course of the ablation phase (Figures 2B and 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figures 2B and 3A.

claim: Frequency did not change in control slices during the ablation phase.
source: Frequency did not change. It measured 0.36 Hz (SD 0.2 Hz, SEM 0.04 Hz) during the detection phase compared to 0.39 Hz (SD 0.3 Hz, SEM 0.01 Hz) during the ablation phase, which was not significant (p=0.49, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with visual evidence in Figure 3B.

claim: Regularity score did not deviate from approximately 1 throughout the ablation phase in control slices.
source: RS did not deviate from ∼1 throughout the ablation phase (Figure 3D, n = 8 slices).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 3D.

claim: Cumulative sequential ablation of Dbx1 ventral respiratory column neurons has no effect on the stability or the period of the respiratory cycle.
source: These data indicate that cumulative sequential ablation of Dbx1 ventral respiratory column neurons has no effect on the stability or the period of the respiratory cycle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in frequency or regularity score in control slices.

claim: The ablation protocol exhausted the entire set of targets in every control experiment without stopping the rhythm.
source: The ablation protocol exhausted the entire set of targets in every control experiment without stopping the rhythm (e.g., 923 confirmed ablations in Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 2B.

claim: Dbx1 preBötC neurons express neurokinin-1 peptide receptors (NK1Rs).
source: Dbx1 preBötC neurons express neurokinin-1 peptide receptors (NK1Rs) (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010) that stimulate respiratory rhythmogenesis (Gray et al., 1999; Pagliardini et al., 2005; Ballanyi and Ruangkittisakul, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010).

claim: NK1Rs stimulate respiratory rhythmogenesis.
source: Dbx1 preBötC neurons express neurokinin-1 peptide receptors (NK1Rs) (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010) that stimulate respiratory rhythmogenesis (Gray et al., 1999; Pagliardini et al., 2005; Ballanyi and Ruangkittisakul, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gray et al., 1999; Pagliardini et al., 2005; Ballanyi and Ruangkittisakul, 2009).

claim: Monoaminergic and peptidergic raphé neurons project to, and receive feedback projections from, the preBötC to elevate excitability in the respiratory network.
source: Monoaminergic and peptidergic raphé neurons project to, and receive feedback projections from, the preBötC to elevate excitability in the respiratory network (Ptak et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Ptak et al., 2009).

claim: Substance P was applied to unlesioned preBötC-surface slices, which transiently increased respiratory frequency.
source: First, as a control, we applied SP to unlesioned preBötC-surface slices, which transiently increased respiratory frequency, i.e., lowered the cycle period from 4.7 s (SD 0.8 s, SEM 0.1 s) to 3.3 s (SD 0.5 s, SEM 0.1 s, average period computed for 25 cycles), and then equilibrated in 21 min (SD 4 min, SEM 2 min, n = 4 slices) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 5A.

claim: The regularity score was approximately 1 throughout the bout in unlesioned slices after SP application.
source: The regularity score was ∼1 throughout the bout, which is consistent with the stable rhythm expected in unlesioned slices (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 5B.

claim: SP transiently revived respiratory rhythm in lesioned preBötC-surface slices.
source: Then, SP was injected into five preBötC-surface slices wherein the cumulative laser ablation of Dbx1 neurons caused 120 s of quiescence. SP transiently revived respiratory rhythm; the average cycle period was 1.7 s (SD 0.4 s, SEM 0.2 s, computed for 10 cycles after SP bolus injection) but the cycle period slowed down rapidly, surpassing the control period previously measured during the detection phase (4.7 s) within 3 min (SD 2 min, SEM 1 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The transient effects of SP were significantly briefer in lesioned slices compared to unlesioned slices.
source: Judged on the basis of equilibration time, the transient effects of SP were significantly briefer in lesioned slices (p=0.02, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Lesioned slices ultimately fell inexorably silent.
source: Furthermore, lesioned slices ultimately fell inexorably silent (Figures 2A and 5C), whereas unlesioned slices maintained rhythmicity for 4–6 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figures 2A and 5C.

claim: Unlesioned slices maintained rhythmicity for 4–6 hr.
source: Furthermore, lesioned slices ultimately fell inexorably silent (Figures 2A and 5C), whereas unlesioned slices maintained rhythmicity for 4–6 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 5A.

claim: The SP-evoked activity in lesioned preBötC-surface slices was irregular with regularity score measuring 2–10.
source: More importantly, the SP-evoked activity in lesioned preBötC-surface slices was irregular: RS measured 2–10 (Figure 5D, compare to unlesioned slice in Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 5D.

claim: The loss of approximately 85 Dbx1 preBötC neurons slows the respiratory oscillator frequency and renders XII motor output nonfunctional.
source: These data indicate that NK1R-expressing Dbx1 neurons can evoke transient cycles of respiratory activity, but the loss of ∼85 Dbx1 preBötC neurons slows the respiratory oscillator frequency and renders XII motor output nonfunctional.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that SP can transiently revive rhythm but it ultimately fails.

claim: The Rubin–Hayes preBötC neuron model was assembled in Erdős-Rényi G(n,p) graphs with population sizes n from 200–400 and connection probabilities p from 0.1 to 0.2.
source: The Rubin–Hayes preBötC neuron model (Rubin et al., 2009) was assembled in Erdős-Rényi G(n,p) graphs (Newman et al., 2006) with population sizes n from 200–400 and connection probabilities p from 0.1 to 0.2.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: Networks within the n–p parameter range that generated respiratory-like cycle periods of approximately 4 s are shown with asterisks in Figure 6A.
source: Networks within the above n–p parameter range that generated respiratory-like cycle periods of ∼4 s are shown with asterisks in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Model networks generated network-wide bursts within 200–300 ms following brief focal glutamatergic stimulation of five or more constituent neurons.
source: This set of model networks also generated network-wide bursts within 200–300 ms following brief focal glutamatergic stimulation of five or more constituent neurons (Figure 6B) in agreement with focal glutamate un-caging experiments in neonatal mouse slices, which showed that simultaneous stimulation of 4–9 preBötC neurons can trigger inspiratory bursts with similar latency (Kam et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data and visual evidence in Figure 6B.

claim: Focal glutamate un-caging experiments in neonatal mouse slices showed that simultaneous stimulation of 4–9 preBötC neurons can trigger inspiratory bursts with similar latency.
source: This set of model networks also generated network-wide bursts within 200–300 ms following brief focal glutamatergic stimulation of five or more constituent neurons (Figure 6B) in agreement with focal glutamate un-caging experiments in neonatal mouse slices, which showed that simultaneous stimulation of 4–9 preBötC neurons can trigger inspiratory bursts with similar latency (Kam et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Kam et al., 2013b).

claim: Sequentially deleting neurons in the model networks decreased frequency until the rhythm stopped altogether.
source: Sequentially deleting neurons in the model networks decreased frequency until the rhythm stopped altogether (Figure 6C,D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data and visual evidence in Figure 6C,D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amplitude of network output did not diminish in simulations.
source: These simulations generally agreed with the experimental results except for two discrepancies. First, the amplitude of network output did not diminish (compare Figure 6C,E to Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data and visual evidence in Figure 6C,E.

claim: Rhythm cessation in simulations required the average deletion of 41 constituent model neurons.
source: Second, rhythm cessation required the average deletion of 41 constituent model neurons (SD 15, SEM 6, range 19–67, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C; Supplementary file 1) as opposed to the experimental cell ablation tally of ∼85.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data and visual evidence in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The cumulative ablation sequence caused no major change in local metrics including cluster coefficient, closeness centrality, and betweenness centrality.
source: From the start to finish, the cumulative ablation sequence caused no major change in local metrics including cluster coefficient, closeness centrality, and betweenness centrality.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of network topology.

claim: Global connectivity metrics such as the K-core showed only modest changes that were incommensurate with the large changes in frequency observed in experiments and simulations.
source: Global connectivity metrics such as the K-core, which has been applied to analyze rhythmic neural systems including the preBötC (Schwab et al., 2010), showed only modest changes that were incommensurate with the large changes in frequency observed in experiments and simulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of network topology.

claim: The number of strongly connected components in the model networks did not depart from unity.
source: The number of strongly connected components in the model networks did not depart from unity, thus the underlying graph was not fractured and every constituent interneuron could be reached via a finite number of synaptic links from every other interneuron, even after the rhythm stopped.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of network topology.

claim: A breakdown in network structure cannot explain the impairment and cessation of rhythmic function.
source: These calculations show that these relatively low numbers of cumulative cellular ablations do not disconnect or disintegrate the core CPG, which suggests that a breakdown in network structure cannot explain the impairment and cessation of rhythmic function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational analysis showing that network connectivity remains intact.

claim: Of the eight Dbx1 neurons with inspiratory modulation, two could be antidromically activated by stimulation within the XII nucleus.
source: Of the eight Dbx1 neurons with inspiratory modulation (Figure 7A–D), two could be antidromically activated by stimulation within the XII nucleus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 7A–D.

claim: Most Dbx1 preBötC neurons are inspiratory and show commissural axons that cross the midline and innervate the contralateral preBötC.
source: Most Dbx1 preBötC neurons are inspiratory and show commissural axons that cross the midline and innervate the contralateral preBötC (Figure 8A–C), as shown previously (Bouvier et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 8A–C and citations to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).

claim: Dbx1 preBötC neurons that are inspiratory modulated send axons ipsilaterally toward the XII nucleus.
source: Here, we identify Dbx1 preBötC neurons that are also inspiratory modulated but send axons ipsilaterally toward the XII nucleus (Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), consistent with a role related to premotor transmission of inspiratory drive from preBötC to XII motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dbx1 preBötC neurons have a role related to premotor transmission of inspiratory drive from preBötC to XII motoneurons.
source: Here, we identify Dbx1 preBötC neurons that are also inspiratory modulated but send axons ipsilaterally toward the XII nucleus (Figure 8D–F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), consistent with a role related to premotor transmission of inspiratory drive from preBötC to XII motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Dbx1 neurons project to the XII nucleus.

claim: Two-photon lasers can destroy cells of a well-defined class with minimal damage to surrounding tissues.
source: Two-photon lasers can destroy cells of a well-defined class with minimal damage to surrounding tissues (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).

claim: An overwhelming majority of Dbx1 neurons in the ventral medulla have a glutamatergic transmitter phenotype and inspiratory modulated firing patterns.
source: An overwhelming majority of Dbx1 neurons in the ventral medulla have a glutamatergic transmitter phenotype and inspiratory modulated firing patterns (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013), so the Cre/lox Dbx1 reporter system is a reliable means to identify neurons with inspiratory function and target them for laser ablation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).

claim: Laser ablation of Dbx1 neurons in the ventral respiratory column had a minor effect on XII motor output amplitude and negligible effects on frequency and regularity.
source: Laser ablation of Dbx1 neurons in the ventral respiratory column had a minor effect on XII motor output amplitude and negligible effects on frequency and regularity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Laser–tissue interactions are not generally deleterious for respiratory function in vitro.
source: These negative results show that laser–tissue interactions are not generally deleterious for respiratory function in vitro (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the negative results in control experiments and supported by citations to prior research (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).

claim: Sequential laser ablation of Dbx1 preBötC neurons steadily diminished the inspiratory burst frequency, caused cycle period fluctuations, and ultimately the cessation of rhythmic motor output.
source: Here, sequential laser ablation of Dbx1 preBötC neurons steadily diminished the inspiratory burst frequency, caused cycle period fluctuations, and ultimately the cessation of rhythmic motor output.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The oscillator was continuously degraded until it could no longer sustain spontaneous function.
source: We conclude that the oscillator was continuously degraded until it could no longer sustain spontaneous function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing progressive degradation of rhythmic function.

claim: Dbx1 knockout mice fail to breathe at birth.
source: These data strengthen the proposal that Dbx1 neurons comprise the core inspiratory rhythm generator, which was originally based on Dbx1 knockout mice that fail to breathe at birth (Pierani et al., 2001), and an array of neuroanatomical and physiological criteria including glutamatergic transmitter phenotype, the expression of peptides and peptide receptors, strong inspiratory rhythmic phenotype, and the ability to synchronize the preBötC bilaterally (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Pierani et al., 2001).

claim: In a previous study, deleting all the detected targets (120 on average) slowed, destabilized, and then stopped the rhythm.
source: We previously laser-ablated rhythmic preBötC neurons identified by Ca2+ imaging. In that study, deleting all the detected targets (120 on average) slowed, destabilized, and then stopped the rhythm (Hayes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Hayes et al., 2012).

claim: The rhythm stopped after a delay of approximately 30 min following the final target ablation in a previous study.
source: In that study, deleting all the detected targets (120 on average) slowed, destabilized, and then stopped the rhythm (Hayes et al., 2012). The interpretability of these experiments suffered two caveats: the rhythm stopped after a delay of ∼30 min following the final target ablation, and furthermore, the transmitter phenotype of the ablated targets was unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Hayes et al., 2012).

claim: Destroying an average of 85 Dbx1 neurons stopped the XII motor rhythm in the midst of the ablation phase, before exhausting the target list.
source: And here, destroying an average of 85 Dbx1 neurons stopped the XII motor rhythm in the midst of the ablation phase, before exhausting the target list, which suggests a more direct impact on the core rhythmogenic circuit.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The preBötC core in vitro is very sensitive to the loss of just a few constituent interneurons (i.e., <100).
source: Here, the debilitating effects on respiratory rhythm generation at a much lower ablation tally suggest that the preBötC core in vitro is very sensitive to the loss of just a few constituent interneurons (i.e., <100).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing rhythm cessation after ~85 ablations.

claim: An acute sensitivity to neuron loss may not apply to the preBötC network in vivo.
source: An acute sensitivity to neuron loss, such as we report for slices, may not apply to the preBötC network in vivo, but this remains to be tested via quantitative cellular ablation experiments with physiological monitoring in intact animal models.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the applicability of in vitro findings to in vivo conditions.

claim: A significant number of detected targets were non-rhythmogenic.
source: We detected an average of 705 Dbx1 target cells in preBötC-surface slices, but we conclude that a significant number were non-rhythmogenic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discrepancy between the number of detected targets and the number of ablations needed to stop rhythm.

claim: Some fraction of detected targets can be discounted as Dbx1-derived non-rhythmogenic glia.
source: Some fraction of the detected targets can be discounted as Dbx1-derived non-rhythmogenic glia (Gray et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Gray et al., 2010).

claim: Some fraction of detected targets manifests premotor function.
source: However, more significantly, some fraction manifests premotor function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing antidromic activation and axonal projections to XII nucleus.

claim: Large-scale pressure ejections of biocytin in the preBötC region of Dbx1-reporter mice labeled many midline-crossing axons as well as axons projecting to the XII nucleus.
source: The present evidence for premotor function in Dbx1 preBötC neurons with verified inspiratory discharge patterns (e.g., Figures 7 and 8D–F) is consistent with large-scale pressure ejections of biocytin in the preBötC region of another strain of Dbx1-reporter mice (Dbx1LacZ knock-in), which labeled many midline-crossing axons as well as axons projecting to the XII nucleus (Bouvier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Bouvier et al., 2010).

claim: A fraction of the excitatory neurons in the preBötC, and immediately dorsal to preBötC, had premotor functionality.
source: Even 20 years ago it was recognized that a fraction of the excitatory neurons in the preBötC, and immediately dorsal to preBötC, had premotor functionality (Funk et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Funk et al., 1993).

claim: A non-negligible fraction of the ablated Dbx1 neurons were inspiratory modulated but non-rhythmogenic, and most likely constitute XII premotor neurons.
source: Because laser ablations in preBötC-surface slices decreased XII magnitude (e.g., Figures 2A and 3A), we propose that a non-negligible fraction of the ablated Dbx1 neurons were inspiratory modulated but non-rhythmogenic, and most likely constitute XII premotor neurons (Peever et al., 2002; Chamberlin et al., 2007; Koizumi et al., 2008; Volgin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing decreased XII amplitude and supported by citations to prior research (Peever et al., 2002; Chamberlin et al., 2007; Koizumi et al., 2008; Volgin et al., 2008).

claim: If each of the two caveats (the existence of Dbx1 glia and premotor neurons) explains approximately 10% of the detected targets, then the size of the essential preBötC core would be N = 564.
source: Although we lack quantitative certainty, if we assume that each of the two caveats above (i.e., the existence of Dbx1 glia and premotor neurons) explains ∼10% of the detected targets, then the size of the essential preBötC core would be N = 705 – 2 [0.1 (705)] = 564, which is remarkably close to the estimate of ∼600 from adult rat studies that enumerated the population size based on NK1R expression in the preBötC (Gray et al., 2001, 1999).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and calculation from the experimental data.

claim: Adult rat studies estimated the population size to be approximately 600 based on NK1R expression in the preBötC.
source: Although we lack quantitative certainty, if we assume that each of the two caveats above (i.e., the existence of Dbx1 glia and premotor neurons) explains ∼10% of the detected targets, then the size of the essential preBötC core would be N = 705 – 2 [0.1 (705)] = 564, which is remarkably close to the estimate of ∼600 from adult rat studies that enumerated the population size based on NK1R expression in the preBötC (Gray et al., 2001, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gray et al., 2001, 1999).

claim: In a previous laser ablation study, population size was estimated to be approximately 325.
source: In our previous laser ablation study, we estimated population size to be ∼325 (Hayes et al., 2012), which probably underestimates the population size because incomplete fluorescent Ca2+ dye loading in slices precludes the detection of a significant fraction of the rhythmogenic preBötC network.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Hayes et al., 2012).

claim: The previous estimate of approximately 325 probably underestimates the population size because incomplete fluorescent Ca2+ dye loading in slices precludes the detection of a significant fraction of the rhythmogenic preBötC network.
source: In our previous laser ablation study, we estimated population size to be ∼325 (Hayes et al., 2012), which probably underestimates the population size because incomplete fluorescent Ca2+ dye loading in slices precludes the detection of a significant fraction of the rhythmogenic preBötC network.
evidence: The claim is inferred from methodological limitations of the previous study.

claim: The preBötC contains rhythmogenic and premotor interneurons that both develop from Dbx1-expressing precursors.
source: Our data suggest that the preBötC contains rhythmogenic and premotor interneurons that both develop from Dbx1-expressing precursors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing both rhythmogenic and premotor functions in Dbx1 neurons.

claim: The role of Dbx1 neurons in spinal locomotor systems is coordinating left–right limb alternation at any speed.
source: It is surprising that Dbx1 neurons play these two roles in respiration when the role of Dbx1 neurons in spinal locomotor systems seems to be coordinating left–right limb alternation at any speed (Lanuza et al., 2004; Talpalar et al., 2013) rather than rhythm generation or premotor transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lanuza et al., 2004; Talpalar et al., 2013).

claim: Dbx1 preBötC neurons appear to have more in common with excitatory Shox2 interneurons of the lumbar spinal cord, which contribute to locomotor rhythm generation and premotor circuits downstream of the rhythm-generating core.
source: In that regard, Dbx1 preBötC neurons appear to have more in common with excitatory Shox2 interneurons of the lumbar spinal cord (a subset of V2 interneurons), which contribute to locomotor rhythm generation and premotor circuits downstream of the rhythm-generating core (Dougherty et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Dougherty et al., 2013).

claim: The ability of Dbx1 preBötC neurons to spontaneously generate rhythmic respiratory motor output in slice preparations is sensitive to deletion of 85 ± 1.96(20) Dbx1 interneurons, i.e., 8–22% of its core.
source: Thus, we conclude the ability of Dbx1 preBötC neurons to spontaneously generate rhythmic respiratory motor output in slice preparations is sensitive to deletion of 85 ± 1.96(20) Dbx1 interneurons, i.e., 8–22% of its core.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The rhythmogenic preBötC core does not appear to be destroyed by piecewise lesioning.
source: Although it cannot function spontaneously post-lesion, the rhythmogenic preBötC core does not appear to be destroyed by piecewise lesioning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SP can transiently evoke activity and network connectivity remains intact.

claim: Peptide injections evoked irregular transient bursts in lesioned preBötC-surface slices.
source: Peptide injections evoked irregular transient bursts in lesioned preBötC-surface slices.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Measures of local and global connectivity in lesioned network models remained undiminished after cumulative cell deletions stopped and precluded rhythmic function.
source: Also, measures of local and global connectivity in lesioned network models remained undiminished after cumulative cell deletions stopped and precluded rhythmic function.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of network topology.

claim: preBötC function depends on non-trivial properties that emerge from non-linear synaptic and intrinsic membrane properties.
source: Therefore, we propose that preBötC function depends on non-trivial properties that emerge from non-linear synaptic and intrinsic membrane properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that network connectivity remains intact but function is lost.

claim: In a group pacemaker, each constituent neuron forms recurrent connections with other constituent neurons in a network of finite size and amplifies excitatory drive via synaptically triggered inward currents.
source: In a group pacemaker, each constituent neuron forms recurrent connections with other constituent neurons in a network of finite size and amplifies excitatory drive via synaptically triggered inward currents (Rekling et al., 1996; Rekling and Feldman, 1998; Rubin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Rekling et al., 1996; Rekling and Feldman, 1998; Rubin et al., 2009).

claim: Arrhythmic respiratory networks retain considerable numbers of constituent neurons and interconnectivity.
source: The likelihood that arrhythmic respiratory networks retain considerable numbers of constituent neurons and interconnectivity suggests that unraveling the cellular and synaptic mechanisms of rhythmogenesis and motor output could be exploited to restore functionality in lesioned slices and, to the extent that our observations apply in vivo, to develop clinical therapies that bolster respiratory function in pathological conditions of animal models or human patients.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the computational analysis showing intact network connectivity after rhythm cessation.

claim: Dbx1 respiratory neurons in the medulla represent excellent potential targets for pharmacological intervention or gene therapy to treat respiratory pathologies.
source: Dbx1 respiratory neurons in the medulla represent excellent potential targets for pharmacological intervention or gene therapy to treat respiratory pathologies.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Enhancing premotor functionality in Dbx1-derived neurons could ameliorate obstructive sleep apnea.
source: Potentially enhancing premotor functionality in Dbx1-derived neurons could ameliorate obstructive sleep apnea.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Boosting the function of rhythmogenic Dbx1 neurons may mitigate central apneas of prematurity as well as opiate respiratory depression.
source: Boosting the function of rhythmogenic Dbx1 neurons may mitigate central apneas of prematurity as well as opiate respiratory depression.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Treatment strategies aimed at rhythmogenic Dbx1 neurons may help overcome the effects of a reduced quantity or efficacy of neurons within the preBötC due to neurodegenerative diseases or aging.
source: Treatment strategies aimed at rhythmogenic Dbx1 neurons may help overcome the effects of a reduced quantity or efficacy of neurons within the preBötC due to neurodegenerative diseases or aging (Benarroch, 2003; Benarroch et al., 2003; Tsuboi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential therapeutic applications and supported by citations to prior research (Benarroch, 2003; Benarroch et al., 2003; Tsuboi et al., 2008).

claim: Transgenic mice express Cre recombinase fused to the tamoxifen-sensitive estrogen receptor (CreERT2) in cells that express the Dbx1 gene.
source: We used transgenic mice that express Cre recombinase fused to the tamoxifen-sensitive estrogen receptor (CreERT2) in cells that express the Dbx1 gene (Dbx1+/CreERT2) (Hirata et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the animal model used in the study and is supported by citations to prior research (Hirata et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013).

claim: Tamoxifen administration to pregnant females on the tenth day after the plug date produces bright native fluorescence in Dbx1-derived neurons in approximately 50% of the offspring.
source: Tamoxifen administration to pregnant females on the tenth day after the plug date produces bright native fluorescence in Dbx1-derived neurons (i.e., Dbx1 neurons) in ∼50% of the offspring: Dbx1+/CreERT2; Rosa26tdTomato.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Anesthesia via hypothermia facilitates the rapid isolation of the intact brainstem and spinal cord.
source: Anesthesia via hypothermia facilitates the rapid isolation of the intact brainstem and spinal cord, which would otherwise be damaged by cervical dislocation.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology and is based on established knowledge about tissue preservation.

claim: A single slice of thickness 400–450 µm invariably retained the preBötC, XII premotor neurons and XII motoneurons that modulate and control airway resistance during breathing.
source: We cut a single slice of thickness 400–450 µm, which invariably retained the preBötC, XII premotor neurons and XII motoneurons that modulate and control airway resistance during breathing.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The external K+ concentration was raised to 9 mM.
source: The external K+ concentration was raised to 9 mM and inspiratory motor output was recorded from XII nerve roots using a suction electrode and an AC-coupled differential amplifier.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Control slices were characterized by the compact division of the nucleus ambiguus (cNA), a thick dorsal inferior olive (IOD), and a minimally developed principal loop of the inferior olive (IOPloop).
source: Control slices were characterized by the compact division of the nucleus ambiguus (cNA), a thick dorsal inferior olive (IOD), and a minimally developed principal loop of the inferior olive (IOPloop).
evidence: The claim describes the anatomical characteristics used to identify control slices.

claim: The preBötC-surface slices were characterized by very little (if any) visible portion of the cNA yet a clear semi-compact nucleus ambiguus (scNA), a fully developed IOPloop, as well as medial inferior olive (IOM).
source: The preBötC-surface slices were characterized by very little (if any) visible portion of the cNA yet a clear semi-compact nucleus ambiguus (scNA), a fully developed IOPloop, as well as medial inferior olive (IOM).
evidence: The claim describes the anatomical characteristics used to identify preBötC-surface slices.

claim: Patch pipettes were fabricated from borosilicate glass with outer diameter 1.5 mm, inner diameter 0.87 mm, and resistance 4–6 MΩ in the bath.
source: Patch pipettes were fabricated from borosilicate glass (OD: 1.5 mm, ID: 0.87 mm, 4–6 MΩ in the bath) and filled with solution containing (in mM): 140 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 1 MgCl2, 0.1 EGTA, 2 Mg-ATP, 0.3 Na-GTP, 50-µM Alexa 488 hydrazide, and 2-mg/ml biocytin.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Empirical measurement of the liquid junction potential was 1 mV and thus not corrected.
source: Empirical measurement of the liquid junction potential was 1 mV and thus not corrected.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Access (series) resistance was approximately 10–15 MΩ, which was countered by bridge balance.
source: Access (series) resistance was ∼10–15 MΩ, which was countered by bridge balance.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Cathodic stimuli were applied at increasing intensities, to a maximum of 0.4 mA, to elicit short latency antidromic action potentials.
source: We applied cathodic stimuli at increasing intensities, to a maximum of 0.4 mA, to elicit short latency antidromic action potentials.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Biocytin-loaded neurons were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M Na-phosphate buffer for at least 16 hr at 4°C.
source: Biocytin-loaded neurons were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M Na-phosphate buffer for at least 16 hr at 4°C.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Slices were treated with Scale solution containing 4 M urea, 10% (mass/volume) glycerol and 0.1% (mass/volume) Triton X-100, for 10 days to clear the tissue and remove opaque background staining.
source: Then, the slices were treated with Scale solution containing 4 M urea, 10% (mass/volume) glycerol and 0.1% (mass/volume) Triton X-100, for 10 days to clear the tissue and remove opaque background staining (Hama et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study and is supported by citation to prior research (Hama et al., 2011).

claim: The instrument incorporated a Zeiss LSM 510 laser scanning head and fixed-stage microscope body with a 20×/1.0 numerical aperture water-immersion objective, an adjustable wavelength 1.5 W Ti:sapphire tunable laser, and a robotic xy translation stage.
source: The instrument incorporated a Zeiss LSM 510 laser scanning head and fixed-stage microscope body with a 20×/1.0 numerical aperture water-immersion objective, an adjustable wavelength 1.5 W Ti:sapphire tunable laser (Spectra Physics, Irvine, CA), and a robotic xy translation stage (Siskiyou Design, Grants Pass OR).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental equipment used in the study.

claim: For neonatal mouse brainstem tissue (P0–5), using 800-nm pulses emitted at approximately 1 W, which measured 36 mW at the specimen plane, the z domain generally measured less than 100 µm.
source: For neonatal mouse brainstem tissue (P0–5), using 800-nm pulses emitted at ∼1 W, which measured 36 mW at the specimen plane, the z domain generally measured less than 100 µm.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Valid Dbx1 neurons in the preBötC and ventral respiratory column pass the circularity test when C exceeds 0.75.
source: Valid Dbx1 neurons in the preBötC and ventral respiratory column pass the circularity test when C exceeds 0.75.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The Ti:sapphire laser scans a 10 square micrometer spot centered on each target with 800-nm pulses at maximum intensity.
source: The Ti:sapphire laser scans a 10 square micrometer spot centered on each target with 800-nm pulses at maximum intensity.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The ablation is confirmed if fluorescence is detected in the band 560–615 nm.
source: The ablation is confirmed if fluorescence is detected in the band 560–615 nm, which reflects presumed water vapor in the cell cavity and excludes infrared reflections of the long-wavelength laser (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by visual evidence in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to prior research (Wang et al., 2013).

claim: Data sets were tested for normality using a Shapiro–Wilk test.
source: Data sets were tested for normality using a Shapiro–Wilk test.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical methodology used in the study.

claim: Data that could be considered normally distributed were compared using two-tailed paired t-tests, whereas data that did not conform to the normal distribution were compared using non-directional (two-tailed) Mann–Whitney U-tests.
source: Data that could be considered normally distributed were compared using two-tailed paired t-tests, whereas data that did not conform to the normal distribution were compared using non-directional (two-tailed) Mann–Whitney U-tests.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical methodology used in the study.

claim: Erdős-Rényi G(n,p)-directed random graphs were generated with key parameters of population size (n) and connection probability (p).
source: We wrote a Matlab (MathWorks Inc., Natick, MA) script to generate Erdős-Rényi G(n,p)-directed random graphs (Newman et al., 2006) with key parameters of population size (n) and connection probability (p).
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology and is supported by citation to prior research (Newman et al., 2006).

claim: A Runge–Kutta fourth-order numerical integration routine with fixed time step of 0.25 ms was used.
source: We used a Runge–Kutta fourth-order numerical integration routine with fixed time step of 0.25 ms.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: Network models were subject to 100 random deletions, one deletion every 25 s.
source: Network models were subject to 100 random deletions, one deletion every 25 s.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: Neuron deletions were achieved by setting the synaptic state variable and its corresponding differential equation to zero.
source: Neuron deletions were achieved by setting the synaptic state variable and its corresponding differential equation to zero, which essentially removes the cell from the network.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: Focal stimulation was achieved by setting the synaptic state variable to 0.9 for 200 ms.
source: Focal stimulation was achieved by setting the synaptic state variable to 0.9 for 200 ms, without modifying the differential equation, so the glutamatergic excitation was indeed transient.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: Population size (n) was varied from 200 to 400 with a step size of 10 and connection probability (p) from 0.1 to 0.2 with a step size of 0.0125.
source: We varied n from 200 to 400 with a step size of 10 and p from 0.1 to 0.2 with a step size of 0.0125.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: For each parameter set, 10 simulations without deletion were conducted for 25 s to assess network rhythmicity.
source: For each parameter set, 10 simulations without deletion were conducted for 25 s to assess network rhythmicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology and is supported by visual evidence in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For parameter sets whose initial period fell between 3 and 4 s, 5–6 simulations with deletions were performed.
source: For the parameter sets whose initial period fell between 3 and 4 s, we performed 5–6 simulations with deletions (for n = 320, 330, 340 we performed 16 simulations in each case) and then calculated the longest period, the ablation tally, and discrete network metrics pertaining to G(n,p).
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: The adjacency matrices are asymmetric for neuronal networks, which are directed.
source: The adjacency matrices are asymmetric for neuronal networks, which are directed (i.e., the chemical synapses are unidirectional).
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology based on established knowledge of neuronal networks.

claim: Three global metrics (K-core, number of strongly connected components, average in and out degree) were computed for the initial network and the remaining network after a sequence of 100 random deletions.
source: We computed three global metrics (K-core, number of strongly connected components, average in and out degree) for the initial network and the remaining network after a sequence of 100 random deletions.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.

claim: For each deleted vertex, three local network metrics (local cluster coefficient, closeness centrality, betweenness centrality) were computed to indicate the importance of the vertex within the previous network.
source: Also for each deleted vertex, we computed three local network metrics (local cluster coefficient, closeness centrality, betweenness centrality) to indicate the importance of the vertex within the previous network.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling methodology used in the study.
